items.prompt: Which printed letter is shown?
items.feedback: The printed shape can match Latin A. In this course it is the Cyrillic vowel letter А.

items.prompt: Which printed letter is shown?
items.feedback: М is an early consonant letter. It is not Н.

items.prompt: This letter looks like Latin P. What is it?
items.feedback: Shape overlap with Latin P is a recognition trap. This is Cyrillic Р, not English P.

items.prompt: This letter looks like Latin H. What is it?
items.feedback: Do not read Н as English H. It is a Cyrillic letter.

items.prompt: This letter looks like Latin C. What is it?
items.feedback: С is a Cyrillic letter. Do not treat the Latin look-alike as the identity.

items.prompt: This letter looks like Latin B. What is it?
items.feedback: В is not Latin B and it is not Cyrillic Б.

items.prompt: This letter looks like Latin Y. What is it?
items.feedback: У is a Cyrillic vowel letter, not Latin Y.

items.prompt: This letter looks like Latin X. What is it?
items.feedback: Х is a Cyrillic letter, not Latin X.

items.prompt: Which printed letter is shown?
items.feedback: Ё is its own letter. Е and Э are different letters.

items.prompt: Which printed letter is shown?
items.feedback: Ю is an iotated vowel letter. У and Я are different letters.

items.prompt: Which printed letter is shown?
items.feedback: Я is an iotated vowel letter. It is not Р or А.

items.prompt: What is the printed letter Й?
options: A consonant letter, not a vowel
items.answer: A consonant letter, not a vowel
items.feedback: Й is not a vowel you read alone and it is not the soft sign.

items.prompt: Which line is one letter written in both print cases?
items.feedback: А / а is one letter. The other lines are two different letters.

items.prompt: Which printed letter is shown?
items.feedback: Е is an iotated vowel letter. Э and Ё are different letters.

items.prompt: What is the printed mark Ь?
options: A vowel you pronounce by itself
A mark, not a standalone vowel
items.answer: A mark, not a standalone vowel
items.feedback: Ь is a sign, not a vowel letter you read alone.

items.prompt: What is the printed mark Ъ?

steps.title: Unit 1 — Printed letters
steps.body: This is a proposed Lesson 1 mapping, not an approved owned-edition alignment. The development unit teaches printed letter identities with public-domain letter forms. Example words and model audio are not part of this unit. Qualified review is still pending.
steps.bookDirection: Open your copy to Lesson 1. Use the book for the author's explanations, exercises, and any example words.

steps.title: Identify letters first
steps.body: Work letter shapes, print pairs, and Latin look-alikes before later reading. Transliteration, if you use it, is a temporary support.

steps.title: Cyrillic is a different alphabet
steps.body: Russian is written with 33 Cyrillic letters. Some printed shapes look like Latin letters and are not the same letters. Learn identity first.

steps.title: First vowel set
steps.body: Work these printed pairs: А а, О о, У у, Э э, Ы ы, И и. English sound notes are pending qualified review.

steps.title: Identify А
steps.body: Choose the Cyrillic identity for the printed letter.

steps.title: Low-confusion consonants

steps.title: Identify М
steps.body: Choose the Cyrillic identity for the printed letter.

steps.title: Shape traps
steps.body: These printed letters often fool Latin-alphabet readers: В, Н, Р, С, У, Х. Name the Cyrillic identity. Read this as a review-pending explanation. Worked examples come before the guided choice, and the independent check is separate. A wrong answer returns to this contrast. Activity is not demonstrated ability.

steps.title: Everyday phrases, naming, and grouping
steps.body: Proposed Unit 3 uses frozen dictionary rows and grammar excerpts for the groups, a small phrase set, and naming items. The owned book remains separate work. Qualified review is pending.
steps.bookDirection: Open Lesson 3 in the copy you own. The app records do not replace that lesson.

steps.title: Read the admitted grouping sentence
steps.body: The frozen page says: So, in Russian, nouns have an intrinsic property called 'gender', which comes in three types: masculine, feminine, and neuter. An ending is not a substitute for the admitted record.

steps.title: Four records in the first group
steps.body: These admitted records are listed as masculine. стол — table. дом — house. го́род — town. брат — brother.

steps.title: Guided practice
steps.body: Choose the admitted record. The feedback states the frozen field.

steps.title: Four records in the second group
steps.body: These admitted records are listed as feminine. кни́га — book. вода́ — water. шко́ла — school. рабо́та — work.

steps.title: Guided practice
steps.body: Choose the admitted record. The feedback states the frozen field.

steps.title: Four records in the third group
steps.body: These admitted records are listed as neuter. окно́ — window. письмо́ — letter. молоко́ — milk. мо́ре — sea.

steps.title: Guided practice
steps.body: Choose the admitted record. The feedback states the frozen field.

steps.title: Two records the page still places in the first group
steps.body: дя́дя and мужчи́на decline like nouns ending in -а, and they are masculine. Say decline for these nouns. Do not say they conjugate.

steps.title: Guided practice
steps.body: Choose the admitted record. The feedback states the frozen field.

steps.title: Remediation
steps.body: дя́дя and мужчи́на decline like nouns ending in -а, and they are masculine. Say decline for these nouns. Do not say they conjugate.

steps.title: My: agreement with the noun
steps.body: In мой стол, стол is masculine singular. In моя собака, собака is feminine singular. Both phrases mean my plus a noun, but the Russian form of my changes to match the noun.

steps.title: Match gender, number and case
steps.body: Possessives such as мо́й and тво́й agree with the noun they describe in gender, number and case. Choose the form from the noun, not from the gender of its owner. Start with the nominative forms below, then compare the feminine accusative example.

steps.title: Our: a worked case change
steps.body: Наш means our; Ваш means your. In the worked phrase на́ша сестра́, both words are feminine singular nominative. To put this phrase in the direct-object accusative, change both words: на́ша сестра́ becomes на́шу сестру́. Keep the same noun and feminine singular agreement. на́шего бра́та changes the referent, and на́ши is plural.

steps.title: Masculine and feminine forms
steps.body: In the nominative singular, мо́й is masculine and моя́ is feminine. For стол choose мо́й; for собака choose моя́. The form follows the noun being described.

steps.title: Neuter and plural forms
steps.body: моё is the neuter singular nominative form of my. мои́ is the plural nominative form. A singular noun does not take the plural form in these choices.

steps.title: Your: masculine and feminine
steps.body: тво́й is masculine singular nominative; твоя́ is feminine singular nominative. Both mean your. To change the masculine form to the feminine form while keeping nominative singular, choose твоя́.

steps.title: Guided practice
steps.body: Choose the form that matches the noun. Then read why the other forms do not fit.

steps.title: Review the agreement rule
steps.body:
Possessives such as мо́й and тво́й agree with the noun they describe in gender, number and case. Choose the form from the noun, not from the gender of its owner. Start with the nominative forms below, then compare the feminine accusative example.

In мой стол, стол is masculine singular. In моя собака, собака is feminine singular. Both phrases mean my plus a noun, but the Russian form of my changes to match the noun.

In the nominative singular, мо́й is masculine and моя́ is feminine. For стол choose мо́й; for собака choose моя́. The form follows the noun being described.

моё is the neuter singular nominative form of my. мои́ is the plural nominative form. A singular noun does not take the plural form in these choices.

Наш means our; Ваш means your. In the worked phrase на́ша сестра́, both words are feminine singular nominative. To put this phrase in the direct-object accusative, change both words: на́ша сестра́ becomes на́шу сестру́. Keep the same noun and feminine singular agreement. на́шего бра́та changes the referent, and на́ши is plural.

тво́й is masculine singular nominative; твоя́ is feminine singular nominative. Both mean your. To change the masculine form to the feminine form while keeping nominative singular, choose твоя́.

steps.title: One adjective, several forms
steps.body: An adjective agrees with its noun in gender, number and case. In хорошее письмо, the adjective describes a neuter singular noun. хоро́ший is the dictionary form: masculine singular nominative. The following forms belong to the same adjective meaning good.

steps.title: Two spelling conditions
steps.body: After ж, ц, ч, ш, or щ, an unstressed о in an ending is written е. That replacement is not a rule for every unstressed о. In хоро́шее, the unstressed ending after ш uses е. The и in хоро́шие follows a different spelling condition: write и rather than ы after ш. Spelling limits the letters in an ending; gender, number and case determine which form is needed.

steps.title: Gender and a worked case change
steps.body: хоро́шая is feminine singular nominative; хоро́шее is neuter singular nominative. In хоро́шая книга, both words are feminine singular nominative. To put the phrase in the accusative singular, change both words: хоро́шая книга becomes хоро́шую книгу. Keep the same noun and feminine singular agreement. хоро́шего друга is masculine animate; хоро́шие книги is plural.

steps.title: Singular, plural and dictionary form
steps.body: хоро́шие is plural nominative. To change хоро́шее from neuter singular nominative to plural nominative, choose хоро́шие. To go back to neuter singular, choose хоро́шее. To supply the dictionary form, choose хоро́ший. These choices test the requested form of the adjective; all the options are already correctly spelled.

steps.title: Guided practice
steps.body: Choose the requested adjective form. Use its gender, number and case, then read the explanation.

steps.title: Review forms and spelling
steps.body:
An adjective agrees with its noun in gender, number and case. In хорошее письмо, the adjective describes a neuter singular noun. хоро́ший is the dictionary form: masculine singular nominative. The following forms belong to the same adjective meaning good.

After ж, ц, ч, ш, or щ, an unstressed о in an ending is written е. That replacement is not a rule for every unstressed о. In хоро́шее, the unstressed ending after ш uses е. The и in хоро́шие follows a different spelling condition: write и rather than ы after ш. Spelling limits the letters in an ending; gender, number and case determine which form is needed.

хоро́шая is feminine singular nominative; хоро́шее is neuter singular nominative. In хоро́шая книга, both words are feminine singular nominative. To put the phrase in the accusative singular, change both words: хоро́шая книга becomes хоро́шую книгу. Keep the same noun and feminine singular agreement. хоро́шего друга is masculine animate; хоро́шие книги is plural.

хоро́шие is plural nominative. To change хоро́шее from neuter singular nominative to plural nominative, choose хоро́шие. To go back to neuter singular, choose хоро́шее. To supply the dictionary form, choose хоро́ший. These choices test the requested form of the adjective; all the options are already correctly spelled.

sessions.title: Recognize nominative forms and plural spelling

steps.title: Singular and plural forms
steps.body: Adjectives agree with their nouns in gender, number and case. In хорошее письмо, the adjective describes a neuter singular noun. хоро́ший is the dictionary form: masculine singular nominative. This lesson compares singular and plural nominative forms, then explains the spelling in the retained plurals.

steps.title: The seven-letter spelling rule
steps.body: After г, к, х, ж, ч, ш, or щ, write и rather than ы. The seven-letter condition is required. This rule applies to the spelling of noun and adjective endings. In кни́ги, и follows г; in хоро́шие, и follows ш. The rule controls spelling, but the question determines the required gender, number and case.

steps.title: A worked noun plural
steps.body: For these nominative checks, кни́га means book in the singular and кни́ги means books in the plural. To form this plural, replace the singular ending with the plural ending: кни́га becomes кни́ги. The stem ends in г, so the seven-letter rule requires и. To return to singular nominative, choose кни́га.

steps.title: Two plural forms, different patterns
steps.body: кни́ги is plural nominative in this lesson. дни is also plural nominative and means days. Its и does not follow a letter in the seven-letter set, so дни is not an example of that spelling replacement. Not every plural ending in и comes from the seven-letter rule. Identify number from the requested form and context.

steps.title: Adjective number and dictionary form
steps.body: хоро́шее is neuter singular nominative; хоро́шие is plural nominative. To change the neuter singular form to plural nominative, choose хоро́шие; to return to neuter singular, choose хоро́шее. For the masculine singular dictionary form, choose хоро́ший. All these options are correctly spelled: the questions test form recognition rather than choosing between correct and incorrect spellings.

sessions.title: Recognize the two taught aspect pairs

steps.title: Aspect and time
steps.body: Aspect describes how an action is viewed, not when it happens. Imperfective can focus on an activity, repetition, or the fact that an action occurred without emphasizing its endpoint. Perfective presents an event with its boundary or result. Imperfective does not by itself mean unfinished. говори́ть is imperfective; сказа́ть is perfective. These infinitives do not specify tense on their own.

steps.title: The saying and telling pair
steps.body: Many Russian verbs are learned in an aspect pair, but not every verb has two words, and a pair is not automatic. говорить and сказать are context-dependent counterparts, not a universal pair for the English verb speak. For the saying/telling pair shown here, the perfective counterpart of говори́ть is сказа́ть; the imperfective counterpart of сказа́ть is говори́ть. These checks ask you to recognize this vocabulary pair, not choose aspect in a sentence.

steps.title: A worked doing and making pair
steps.body: де́лать is imperfective; сде́лать is perfective. Both concern doing or making. The perfective focuses on accomplishing the action; the imperfective can describe the activity or its occurrence without that focus. Given де́лать and a request for its perfective counterpart, choose сде́лать. говори́ть concerns speaking or saying and belongs to the other pair. Learn the shown pair rather than assuming every prefix changes only aspect.

steps.title: Guided practice
steps.body: Choose the counterpart from the saying/telling pair. Then compare its aspect and meaning with the other option.

steps.title: Review the two aspect pairs
steps.body:

These infinitives do not specify tense on their own.

steps.title: Guided practice
steps.body: Choose the admitted record. The feedback states the frozen field.

steps.title: Admitted instruction
steps.body: In English, when reporting a story, we usually change the tense of what was said: compare "I ''am'' English" with "He said he ''was'' English" - the reported verb changes tense. In Russian, however, we keep the tense the same, so the same report is literally, "He said he '''is''' English" - "'''Он сказа́л, что он англича́нин'''", not "'''Он сказа́л, что он ''был'' англича́нином'''".

steps.title: Remediation
steps.body: In English, when reporting a story, we usually change the tense of what was said: compare "I ''am'' English" with "He said he ''was'' English" - the reported verb changes tense. In Russian, however, we keep the tense the same, so the same report is literally, "He said he '''is''' English" - "'''Он сказа́л, что он англича́нин'''", not "'''Он сказа́л, что он ''был'' англича́нином'''".

objectives.title: Recognize verbs used with instrumental complements

steps.title: Admitted instrumental rows
steps.body: Proposed Unit 16 uses frozen instrumental rows and the admitted complement span. Qualified review is pending.
steps.bookDirection: Open Lesson 16 in the copy you own. The app records do not replace that lesson.

steps.title: One noun, different cases
steps.body: The instrumental case can mark the means used to do something. These checks first teach its forms. сто́л is the dictionary form, meaning table; столо́м is instrumental singular. The word still names a table: the ending marks its grammatical role, not a new vocabulary meaning.

steps.title: A bounded noun ending
steps.body: The instrumental singular -ом fits the hard stem of the relevant noun class. Soft stems use their own instrumental ending, so -ом is not universal. Here, keep the stem of сто́л and add -ом to obtain столо́м. Learn the stress with the whole form.

steps.title: Compare the other cases
steps.body: столу́ is dative singular and столе́ is prepositional singular. Both belong to the same noun, but neither has the instrumental singular ending. For an instrumental singular request, select столо́м rather than selecting a form merely because its English gloss is table.

steps.title: Work the house form
steps.body: до́м means house in its dictionary form. до́мом is instrumental singular: keep the stem and add -ом. Given до́м and an instrumental singular request, choose до́мом. This is the same ending pattern as the table form.

steps.title: Check case before choosing
steps.body: до́му is dative singular; до́ме is prepositional singular. They do not answer an instrumental singular request. Compare the entire ending with до́мом, and notice that this noun keeps its stem stress.

steps.title: Meaning and form together
steps.body: поездом is instrumental singular of the noun meaning train; карандашом is instrumental singular of the noun meaning pencil. The pencil check asks for that meaning as well as the case. Its other options refer to train and husband. A correct case alone does not identify the requested noun.

steps.title: A different singular pattern
steps.body: книгой is the instrumental singular form for book. This noun has a different ending from the -ом shown for table and house. Do not attach the same ending to every noun. These examples introduce selected singular patterns, not the full instrumental paradigm.

steps.title: Guided practice
steps.body: Identify the requested case and number, then compare the displayed forms. A missed check returns to the full explanation and examples.

steps.title: Review the instrumental contrasts
steps.body:

столу́ is dative singular and столе́ is prepositional singular. Both belong to the same noun, but neither has the instrumental singular ending. For an instrumental singular request, select столо́м rather than selecting a form merely because its English gloss is table.

до́м means house in its dictionary form. до́мом is instrumental singular: keep the stem and add -ом. Given до́м and an instrumental singular request, choose до́мом. This is the same ending pattern as the table form.

до́му is dative singular; до́ме is prepositional singular. They do not answer an instrumental singular request. Compare the entire ending with до́мом, and notice that this noun keeps its stem stress.

поездом is instrumental singular of the noun meaning train; карандашом is instrumental singular of the noun meaning pencil. The pencil check asks for that meaning as well as the case. Its other options refer to train and husband. A correct case alone does not identify the requested noun.

книгой is the instrumental singular form for book. This noun has a different ending from the -ом shown for table and house. Do not attach the same ending to every noun. These examples introduce selected singular patterns, not the full instrumental paradigm.

steps.title: Independent checks
steps.body: Identify the requested case and number, then compare the displayed forms. A missed check returns to the full explanation and examples.

steps.title: Instrumental plural of book
steps.body: Instrumental plural refers to more than one. кни́га is the dictionary singular form for book; кни́гами is instrumental plural. Keep the stem and use -ами in this pattern. Given an instrumental plural request, choose кни́гами.

steps.title: Plural noun endings
steps.body: Instrumental plural nouns commonly use -ами or -ями, with exceptions. The book, house and table forms shown here use -ами. This is a noun ending; adjectives have their own agreement endings. These checks ask you to recognize the displayed pattern, not derive every noun form.

steps.title: Compare plural cases
steps.body: кни́гам is dative plural; кни́гах is prepositional plural. Neither is instrumental plural. Compare their endings with кни́гами: the final vowel is part of the instrumental plural ending here.

steps.title: Work the house plural
steps.body: до́м names a house in the dictionary singular. дома́ми is instrumental plural. For this plural case request choose дома́ми, including the stress shown in the retained form.

steps.title: Case and number both matter
steps.body: дома́м is dative plural. до́мом is instrumental singular. The first has the wrong case; the second has the right case but the wrong number for an instrumental plural request. дома́ми meets both requirements.

steps.title: Work the table plural
steps.body: сто́л is the dictionary singular form for table. стола́ми is instrumental plural. For an instrumental plural request, select стола́ми and learn its stress with the ending.

steps.title: Reject a singular instrumental
steps.body: стола́м is dative plural; столо́м is instrumental singular. Neither meets both parts of an instrumental plural request. стола́ми supplies instrumental case and plural number together.

steps.title: Guided practice
steps.body: Identify the requested case and number, then compare the displayed forms. A missed check returns to the full explanation and examples.

steps.title: Review the instrumental contrasts
steps.body:
Instrumental plural refers to more than one. кни́га is the dictionary singular form for book; кни́гами is instrumental plural. Keep the stem and use -ами in this pattern. Given an instrumental plural request, choose кни́гами.

Instrumental plural nouns commonly use -ами or -ями, with exceptions. The book, house and table forms shown here use -ами. This is a noun ending; adjectives have their own agreement endings. These checks ask you to recognize the displayed pattern, not derive every noun form.

кни́гам is dative plural; кни́гах is prepositional plural. Neither is instrumental plural. Compare their endings with кни́гами: the final vowel is part of the instrumental plural ending here.

до́м names a house in the dictionary singular. дома́ми is instrumental plural. For this plural case request choose дома́ми, including the stress shown in the retained form.

дома́м is dative plural. до́мом is instrumental singular. The first has the wrong case; the second has the right case but the wrong number for an instrumental plural request. дома́ми meets both requirements.

сто́л is the dictionary singular form for table. стола́ми is instrumental plural. For an instrumental plural request, select стола́ми and learn its stress with the ending.

стола́м is dative plural; столо́м is instrumental singular. Neither meets both parts of an instrumental plural request. стола́ми supplies instrumental case and plural number together.

steps.title: Independent checks
steps.body: Identify the requested case and number, then compare the displayed forms. A missed check returns to the full explanation and examples.

steps.title: Adjective agreement
steps.body: An adjective agrees with its noun in case and number, and in gender in the singular. хоро́ший is the masculine dictionary form for good. хоро́шим is its masculine or neuter instrumental singular form. Here the check requests masculine instrumental; it does not ask for an English gloss.

steps.title: Adjective endings differ
steps.body: Hard-stem masculine and neuter adjectives take -ым in the instrumental, and the soft or spelling-restricted stems take -им. These are adjective declension endings. хоро́шим uses -им because of the spelling restriction after its stem-final consonant. Do not apply the noun ending -ом to this adjective.

steps.title: Compare dative and plural
steps.body: хоро́шему is dative masculine or neuter singular. хоро́шие is nominative plural. Neither is the masculine instrumental singular form requested here. Work the choice by selecting хоро́шим.

steps.title: Instrumental plural agreement
steps.body: хоро́шими is instrumental plural, with a plural adjective ending. хоро́шая is feminine nominative singular. For a plural instrumental request select хоро́шими; хоро́шим has singular number. Recognizing these forms does not by itself demonstrate using adjective agreement in a sentence.

steps.title: Guided practice
steps.body: Identify the requested case and number, then compare the displayed forms. A missed check returns to the full explanation and examples.

steps.title: Review the instrumental contrasts
steps.body:
An adjective agrees with its noun in case and number, and in gender in the singular. хоро́ший is the masculine dictionary form for good. хоро́шим is its masculine or neuter instrumental singular form. Here the check requests masculine instrumental; it does not ask for an English gloss.

Hard-stem masculine and neuter adjectives take -ым in the instrumental, and the soft or spelling-restricted stems take -им. These are adjective declension endings. хоро́шим uses -им because of the spelling restriction after its stem-final consonant. Do not apply the noun ending -ом to this adjective.

хоро́шему is dative masculine or neuter singular. хоро́шие is nominative plural. Neither is the masculine instrumental singular form requested here. Work the choice by selecting хоро́шим.

steps.title: Two meanings of with

Here with introduces the person involved in the meeting: this is the accompaniment line, using a preposition followed by instrumental forms.

steps.title: What a complement describes

steps.title: Position rather than quantity
steps.body: пе́рвый — first. второ́й — second. тре́тий — third. четвёртый — fourth. An ordinal identifies position in an ordered sequence; a cardinal tells how many. These isolated ordinal forms are masculine nominative singular. Learn the position expressed by each form before choosing it.

steps.title: Ordinals agree like adjectives
steps.body: Ordinals agree with their noun in gender, number and case, like adjectives. восемнадцатую девушку means the eighteenth girl as a feminine accusative noun phrase. The retained example comes from a sentence about photographing her; this displayed fragment alone does not mean She just photographed. The ordinal ending follows the noun phrase, rather than staying in the masculine dictionary form. These recognition checks do not assess producing agreement in a sentence.

Read the English request: the separately shown Russian cue may name a different position and is not the target to copy.

sessions.title: Recognize hour counts and noun forms

steps.title: One, two and five hours
steps.body: один час — one hour. два часа — two hours. пять часов — five hours. The noun changes with the count: nominative singular after one, genitive singular after two, and genitive plural after five. English uses hours for both two and five, but Russian uses different forms.

steps.title: Bound the counting rule
steps.body: For basic counts in nominative or inanimate accusative constructions, use the one pattern for numbers ending in 1, the two pattern for endings 2, 3 or 4, and the five pattern for endings 0, 5, 6, 7, 8 or 9. Numbers ending in 11, 12, 13 or 14 take the five pattern instead. Other case constructions require additional changes to the numeral and noun; this is not a rule for every sentence position.

steps.title: Work an hour choice

Recognizing these hour counts does not demonstrate telling the time on a clock.

sessions.title: Interpret quarter, half and time remaining

steps.title: A quarter into the next named hour
steps.body: четверть восьмого — 7:15. The eighth hour is the period leading up to eight, not the period starting at eight. A quarter of that hour has elapsed after seven. The ordinal names the next hour and appears in genitive form.

steps.title: Half of the hour in progress
steps.body: полвосьмого — 7:30. Half of the eighth hour has passed, so the clock shows half past seven. The compact half-hour expression is written as one word in this retained form. Match the construction to the clock reading, rather than treating the named eighth hour as the elapsed whole hour.

steps.title: A quarter remaining before eight

The without construction differs from counting a quarter or a half already elapsed. These choices interpret existing forms; context is still needed to distinguish morning from evening.

steps.title: Comparing a quality
steps.body: бо́льший — bigger. лу́чший — better. These retained forms concern degree of a quality, rather than naming an unrelated object. The first compares size. The second is the source gloss used by the existing choice; it can mean best in context, so better here is not a universal translation. These full adjective forms can change for gender, number and case; they are not the same construction as an unchanging short comparative. Qualified review of the contextual gloss remains pending.

steps.title: One-word and two-word comparisons
steps.body: красне́е — redder. бо́лее до́брый — kinder. The first is a short comparative with an ending expressing a higher degree of redness; this short form does not change for gender, number or case. The second combines a word meaning more with the ordinary long adjective meaning kind. In this two-word construction the adjective still changes for agreement. Not every adjective has a one-word comparative, and these examples do not give a complete formation rule for unfamiliar adjectives.

steps.title: Comparative versus superlative
steps.body: наибо́льший — the biggest. This retained superlative identifies the greatest size in the relevant group, rather than just a greater degree. Contrast the source labels бо́лее — more, ме́нее — less, and наиме́нее — least. More and less express comparison; least identifies the lowest degree. For наибо́льший select the biggest, not more or less. For бо́лее до́брый select kinder, not least or bigger. These choices recognize existing forms; they do not assess independently forming new comparisons or a complete comparison sentence.

sessions.title: Distinguish which questions from relative clauses

steps.title: Questions selecting an apple or a book
steps.body: Которое яблоко моё? — Which apple is mine? Которую книгу вы хотите? — Which book do you want? These are direct questions asking which member is selected, not relative clauses modifying an earlier noun. In the apple question the selecting form agrees with a neuter singular subject in the nominative. In the book question it agrees with a feminine singular direct object in the accusative. Match the whole question: ownership of an apple differs from wanting a book.

steps.title: A relative clause adds information about a noun
steps.body: Человек, который изменил мир — The man who changed the world. The clause following the comma describes the preceding person; it does not ask which person. The relative form takes masculine singular agreement from that noun, and nominative case because it is the subject of changed inside its own clause. For a relative form, gender and number come from the noun it describes; case comes from the role inside the relative clause, not automatically from the preceding noun.

steps.title: With whom: a preposition inside the relative clause
steps.body: Же́нщина, с кото́рой я дружу́ — The woman (who) I'm friends with. The relative clause describes the woman. Its relative form has feminine singular agreement and instrumental case after the preposition meaning with. Russian keeps this preposition before the relative form, while the retained English rendering places with at the end. Compare the woman described by friendship with the man described by changing the world and the two direct questions. Recognizing these meanings does not demonstrate independently choosing a relative case or producing a new clause.

steps.title: Admitted prefix cautions

sessions.title: Distinguish changed meanings and genuine aspect partners

steps.title: Different prefixes can change the meaning
steps.body: отговорить — to dissuade. договориться — to agree. These are different meanings, even though the words share material with a verb of speaking. A prefix is not always just an aspect marker: learn the whole verb and its meaning.

steps.title: The actual dissuade aspect pair
steps.body: отговаривать is the imperfective partner of perfective отговорить: both concern dissuading. The retained source explicitly identifies this pair. сказать belongs to a separate speaking pair; it is not the imperfective partner of отговорить. For a question asking for the perfective partner of отговаривать, select отговорить. договориться is a different verb meaning to agree.

steps.title: Keep the other meanings separate
steps.body: написать — to write. сделать — to do. Neither expresses dissuading or agreeing. When a question asks for a meaning, translate the displayed verb. When it asks for an aspect partner, preserve the lexical meaning while changing aspect. These selections do not demonstrate creating new prefixed verbs or using aspect in a sentence.

sessions.title: Interpret conditional structure and speaker agreement

steps.title: The past form with a conditional particle
steps.body: я спал бы is used by a male speaker; я спала́ бы is used by a female speaker. These labels describe the speaker marked by the past-form agreement; they are not translations of the whole expressions. Both use the first-person pronoun, a past-form verb and the conditional particle. In this construction the past form need not report an actual past event: it can express a hypothetical situation, such as I would sleep. Context supplies the time reference.

steps.title: Read agreement rather than an English sentence label
steps.body: Compare the two retained forms я спал бы and я спала́ бы. The feminine past form has a final vowel that the masculine form lacks. For the first choose a male speaker; for the second choose a female speaker. I would like to sleep is a sentence meaning, not a label identifying the gender marked by the shown past form. steps.title: A wish and a different position for the particle
steps.body: я бы поспа́л — I would like to sleep. я бы поспала́ has feminine speaker agreement: the speaker is marked feminine. The first-person pronoun identifies the speaker, rather than another person. These retained wish expressions have the conditional particle before the verb, whereas the earlier examples put it after the verb. It cannot begin its clause. The wish reading comes from the construction and context, not from translating every conditional particle as would like. sessions.title: Distinguish motion meaning, directionality and setting out

steps.title: Walking and travelling by vehicle
steps.body: идти́ — to go, walk. е́хать — to go by vehicle, ride. The first describes movement on foot; the second movement by vehicle. These are different means of moving, not an aspect pair.

steps.title: Directionality is separate from aspect
steps.body: The table places идти́ in the unidirectional column: motion in one direction. Its other column is multidirectional, covering repeated, return or different-direction movement according to context. These directionality labels are not English verb meanings. The basic unprefixed forms in these columns are imperfective; unidirectional does not itself mean perfective or arrival.

steps.title: Carrying, leading and transporting
steps.body: нести́ — to carry. вести́ — to lead. везти́ — to convey, transport. Carrying on foot, leading someone and transporting by vehicle are distinct meanings. For нести́ choose to carry. A question about its meaning is different from a question about directionality.

steps.title: Setting out does not assert arrival
steps.body: Он пошёл к другу. — he set off toward a friend. The perfective prefixed verb presents the beginning of the journey; it does not say that he arrived. Он шёл к другу. — He went to a friend's place. This retained English rendering accompanies an imperfective form describing motion toward the friend; the Russian form alone does not specify how long he was on the way. The distractor he was already on the way for a long time adds duration that is not supplied, and he refused to go contradicts the setting-out sentence.

steps.title: Read the path and only the displayed clause
steps.body: Мальчик отошёл от незнакомца — The boy stepped back from the stranger. The verb and the phrase after it express movement away from the stranger. There is no additional relative clause in this displayed sentence. Они у́летят из Владивостока через месяц. — They will leave Vladivostok in a month. Мяч залетел на крышу дома. — The ball flew onto the roof of the house. These are different subjects and paths. The prefix contributes to the motion meaning, while the accompanying phrases identify the path and time; do not substitute a translation of a different example.

steps.title: Admitted object and purpose lines

sessions.title: Connect own possession to the subject and the possessed noun

steps.title: Who owns it and which noun controls the form
steps.body: The reflexive possessive refers to the subject as the owner. Its gender, number and case agree with the possessed noun, not with the owner. The retained dictionary forms are свой, своя, своё and свои. A masculine owner and a feminine owner can therefore use the same possessive form with the same noun.

steps.title: The movie belongs to the subject
steps.body: Бо́ря рассказа́л о своём люби́мом фи́льме. — (Borya told about his favorite movie.). А́нна рассказа́ла о своём люби́мом фи́льме. — (Anna told about her favorite movie.). In each sentence the favorite movie belongs to the subject. The movie noun has the same gender, number and case in both, so the possessive form stays the same. The name and past-verb agreement change. The exercise asks you to preserve that movie object while changing the subject.

steps.title: The same own book with two subjects
steps.body: Свое́й кни́ги она́ никогда́ не написа́ла. — (She never wrote her own book.). Свое́й кни́ги он никогда́ не написа́л. — (He never wrote his own book.). The possessive agrees with the feminine singular book noun; the shown form is genitive in this negative sentence. Changing the subject changes the past verb's agreement, not the book phrase. These sentences are about a book, not a movie or jeans.

steps.title: Plural jeans and the limits of the checks
steps.body: Бо́ря наде́л свои́ джи́нсы. — (Borya put on his own jeans.). А́нна наде́ла свои́ джи́нсы. — (Anna put on her own jeans.). Plural jeans require plural possessive agreement regardless of whether Borya or Anna owns them. The exercise keeps this object and changes the subject. The checks select supplied matched sentences; they do not demonstrate independently declining the possessive or constructing an ownership sentence.

sessions.title: Distinguish oneself from a possessed object

steps.title: The person loved and the person who owns
steps.body: Я люблю́ себя́ — I love myself. Я люблю́ (свою́) жену́ — I love my wife. In the first sentence the object refers back to the subject. In the second the object is a wife; the parenthesized possessive makes ownership explicit. Loving oneself and loving a wife describe different objects.

steps.title: A whole sentence is more than its object word
steps.body: жену́ is the accusative form of the noun meaning wife. It does not mean I love. In Я люблю́ свою́ жену́ the verb supplies loving and the noun supplies its object. The full displayed sentence Я люблю́ (свою́) жену́ means I love my wife; the full displayed sentence Я люблю́ себя́ means I love myself. Choose the whole-sentence meaning rather than translating the object word as the verb. These checks recognize two retained sentences; they do not demonstrate independently choosing every reflexive case form.

жену́ is the accusative form of the noun meaning wife. It does not mean I love. In Я люблю́ свою́ жену́ the verb supplies loving and the noun supplies its object. The full displayed sentence Я люблю́ (свою́) жену́ means I love my wife; the full displayed sentence Я люблю́ себя́ means I love myself. Choose the whole-sentence meaning rather than translating the object word as the verb. These checks recognize two retained sentences; they do not demonstrate independently choosing every reflexive case form.

sessions.title: Distinguish purpose, condition, cause and concession

steps.title: Purpose and condition
steps.body: чтобы — so that. если — if. The first conjunction can introduce a purpose; the second introduces a condition. In a purpose construction with the same subject for both actions, an infinitive after the purpose conjunction can name the intended action. This rule is explained here, but the current choices do not require composing such a sentence.

steps.title: Ordinary purpose wording
steps.body: чтобы is an ordinary purpose conjunction. The bookish or archaic qualifier in the retained source belongs to дабы, not to чтобы. The English meaning so that differs from the conditional if and the causal because. Select the meaning of the displayed conjunction; do not infer an archaic register for the ordinary form.

steps.title: Cause, concession and time
steps.body: потому что — because. хотя — although. The first gives a reason; the second introduces a concession. The English label after names a temporal relationship rather than a reason. English since can also express a reason, so it is not a contrasting wrong answer to because in this exercise. The causal check instead contrasts because with although and after. These conjunction meanings are distinct from purpose and condition.

sessions.title: Connect quantity to gender and noun case

steps.title: One agrees with its noun
steps.body: один мальчик — one boy. одна девушка — one girl. The numeral meaning one agrees with its noun in gender, number and case. These displayed counting phrases use a singular noun: the masculine boy takes the masculine numeral, and the feminine girl takes the feminine numeral. The guided choice asks for another phrase with one, not the same noun.

steps.title: The scope of the counting rule
steps.body: For nominative counting phrases, one takes a singular noun, two through four take a genitive singular noun, and five through twenty take a genitive plural noun. Apply this shortcut to an accusative phrase only where its forms coincide with the nominative. Animate accusative phrases and other cases need their own case forms; the shortcut is not a rule that all number phrases keep these endings.

steps.title: Two, three and four form a group
steps.body: две девушки — two girls. три кошки — three cats. Both displayed nouns are genitive singular after these numerals, although the quantity is greater than one and these endings can resemble nominative plural. The numeral for two has a feminine form; the form for three does not change for the noun gender. The check asks for another example in the two-through-four group, not an English translation of the cue.

steps.title: Five and higher in the displayed group
steps.body: пять девушек — five girls. десять копеек — ten kopeks. Here the nouns are genitive plural. Five and ten belong to the same noun-form group; one and two do not. Numbers whose last two digits are 11 through 14 also use this group, including 111 through 114. These choices recognize supplied number phrases; they do not test independently producing every noun ending.

steps.title: Three endings in compound quantities

In these nominative counting phrases, 33 ends in three and takes a genitive singular noun; 41 ends in one and takes a singular noun. The choice may ask for a different final-digit group from the displayed reference phrase. Read the requested group in the question.

steps.title: Check the last two digits first
steps.body: For these whole-number counting phrases, check the last two digits before the final digit. Endings 11 through 14 require genitive plural. Otherwise a final one takes singular, final two through four take genitive singular, and final zero or five through nine take genitive plural. For example, 111 differs from 41; 113 differs from 33. These are numeric rule comparisons, not newly supplied Russian phrases. In other cases the numeral and noun need the relevant declined forms.

sessions.title: Distinguish dative, instrumental and prepositional numeral forms

steps.title: A changed form can name a different case
steps.body: двум — Дательный, the dative. двумя — Творительный, the instrumental. Both are declined forms of the numeral meaning two. Dative commonly marks a recipient or goal; instrumental can mark accompaniment or means. The final part of the form distinguishes these two shown examples; it is not enough to recognize the quantity two.

steps.title: Read a row in its case context
steps.body: Дательный means dative; Творительный means instrumental; Предложный means prepositional. A form must be interpreted with its construction. The bare form двух can occur in more than one case. The admitted row includes the preposition and is labelled prepositional; the check does not claim that a bare ending always uniquely identifies a case. In oblique number phrases the plural noun normally carries the case required by the construction.

steps.title: The displayed prepositional row
steps.body: (о) двух / (об) обоих / (о) полутора — Предложный. This complete row gives the prepositional forms for two, both and one and a half. The parentheses show the accompanying preposition; it is not part of the numeral itself. The prepositional choice contrasts with the dative двум and instrumental двумя. Recognizing this row does not demonstrate independently declining a complete number phrase.

sessions.title: Connect both to gender and case

steps.title: Dative both has two gender forms
steps.body: обеим — Дательный. обоим — Дательный. Both forms mean both in the dative. The feminine series has the stem seen in обеим; the masculine/neuter series has the stem seen in обоим. Gender refers to the counted noun. Changing the gender series does not change the case: both displayed forms are dative.

steps.title: Meaning, gender and the dative row
steps.body: Both refers to the full pair, rather than an unspecified quantity of two. The retained nominative table distinguishes masculine/neuter and feminine forms. The dative row двум / обеим / полутора places two, feminine both and one and a half together by case, not by equal meaning. Дательный is dative, Творительный is instrumental, and Предложный is prepositional.

steps.title: Instrumental adds a different case contrast
steps.body: обеими — Творительный. обоими — Творительный. The feminine and masculine/neuter series remain distinct, but both shown forms are instrumental. Compare обеим with обеими and обоим with обоими: the extra final vowel distinguishes these dative and instrumental examples. The current choices check the case of a supplied form; they do not test producing the correct gender-and-case form in a new sentence.

sessions.title: Explain gender, case and the noun after one and a half

steps.title: One and a half changes for gender
steps.body: полтора́ рубля́ — 1.5 roubles. полторы́ мину́ты — 1.5 minutes. The first numeral form is masculine/neuter; the second is feminine. In the nominative and accusative construction, one and a half takes a genitive singular noun. The noun determines the numeral gender even though the amount exceeds one. The retained alternative gloss one and a half hours / an hour and a half names hours, not roubles or minutes.

steps.title: The oblique form does not fix the noun ending
steps.body: In the other cases, the numeral has the shared form полутора, and the noun is plural in the case required by the construction. The numeral form alone therefore cannot tell you whether a phrase is genitive, dative or instrumental. Compare the preposition and the noun ending. This differs from the genitive singular noun after the nominative/accusative forms.

steps.title: From, to and with have different constructions
steps.body: из полу́тора рубле́й — from 1.5 roubles: the preposition requires genitive plural on the noun. к полу́тора рубля́м — to 1.5 roubles: the preposition requires dative plural. The English distractor with 1.5 roubles names accompaniment/means with an instrumental noun in the corresponding retained source construction. The amount stays one and a half while the preposition changes the relationship. The check asks for the meaning of the whole shown phrase, including from or to.

sessions.title: Distinguish cardinal, ordinal and collective number forms

steps.title: Two and three as collective quantities
steps.body: два — дво́е. три — тро́е. A cardinal states a quantity; a collective presents that quantity as a group. An ordinal states position in a sequence. Thus дво́е is the collective for two, and тро́е is the collective for three. The option второ́й means second, and тре́тий means third; these are ordinal positions, not collective quantities.

steps.title: Collectives have restricted uses
steps.body: Collective number forms are not a general replacement for cardinal numbers with every noun. Standard uses include groups of male people, children or people expressed by appropriate group nouns, personal pronouns, and certain nouns used only in the plural. Use ordinary cardinals with female-person nouns in standard usage; do not infer that any feminine noun takes a collective. This lesson explains the restriction without introducing new Russian noun combinations.

steps.title: Four and the limits of these checks
steps.body: четы́ре — че́тверо. The collective form keeps the quantity four while presenting it as a group. The ordinal distractor четвёртый means fourth, a position; дво́е is a group of two. In the earlier check, че́тверо is a collective but has the wrong quantity for three. Selecting the collective column does not demonstrate choosing its use with every noun or constructing a declined collective phrase.

sessions.title: Read decade ranges in their century context

steps.title: A decade is a range of years
steps.body: В шестидесятых годах — in the 1960s. В девяностых годах — in the 1990s. These expressions refer to decade ranges rather than a single year. The ordinal describing the decade and the noun meaning years are in the prepositional plural. The two displayed choices distinguish the sixties from the nineties.

steps.title: The century comes from context
steps.body: Here the supplied English glosses assume the twentieth century. A decade expression by itself does not fix the century in every context; an explicit century or the surrounding discussion can identify it. Read the decade word, not just the shared ending for years. The checks recognize these two supplied ranges; they do not test forming a new decade expression.

sessions.title: Locate the beginning, middle or end of a period

steps.title: The end of a year and the beginning of a century
steps.body: В конце года — at the end of the year. В начале века — at the beginning of the century. The position word identifies which part of the period is meant, while the following noun identifies the period. Both parts matter: an end is not a beginning, and a year is not a century.

steps.title: The two nouns have different case roles
steps.body: In these expressions, the location noun after the preposition is prepositional, and the noun naming the period is genitive. The English of relationship links the part to the larger period. Do not assign one case to both nouns simply because they appear in the same time phrase.

steps.title: The middle of the week
steps.body: В середине недели — in the middle of the week. This locates an event within the central part of a week; it does not mean the end of a year or the beginning of a century. The checks match complete supplied expressions, not independently produced period-and-position combinations.

sessions.title: Place one action during another event

steps.title: An event supplies the time frame
steps.body: Она родилась во время войны. — She was born during the war. Во время поездки я познакомился с новыми друзьями. — During the trip I met new friends. The war and trip are the surrounding events during which the birth and meeting happen. During does not mean that the birth or meeting continued for the entire war or trip.

steps.title: Meaning and case of the surrounding event
steps.body: The compound preposition meaning during takes the event noun in the genitive. Match the whole sentence: birth during a war differs from meeting friends during a trip. This expresses when an event happens within another event, not the time needed to complete a task. The supplied translations do not demonstrate constructing every during-an-event sentence.

sessions.title: Read the interval over which activity occurs

steps.title: A lesson and a day as intervals
steps.body: В течение урока ученики работали над проектом. — Throughout the lesson, the students worked on the project. В течение дня погода менялась несколько раз. — During the course of the day, the weather changed several times. The interval contains the activity or repeated events. Project work over the lesson does not by itself assert that the project was finished.

steps.title: Duration does not require an unbroken event
steps.body: It emphasizes the duration over which something occurs. The compound preposition takes a genitive noun naming the interval. The weather example explicitly describes several changes during the day, so the expression need not mean one continuous unchanged action. Compare the whole proposition as well as the interval: students and a project differ from weather changes. These checks identify supplied meanings, not task-completion time.

sessions.title: Distinguish before, after, in a period and ago

steps.title: Before and after a reference event
steps.body: Перед ужином мы ходили в парк. — before. После работы я смотрела фильм. — after. The first places the park visit earlier than dinner; the second places watching a film later than work. The preposition meaning before takes an instrumental noun; the one meaning after takes a genitive noun. The English labels classify only this time relation, not the full sentence translation.

steps.title: A time point is different from a duration
steps.body: The future-looking in expression locates an event after an interval from the reference time. Ago locates an event before the reference time. Neither meaning alone states how long the activity lasts or how long it takes to finish a task. Before and after a named event likewise express order relative to that event, not completion.

steps.title: The forward and backward interval examples
steps.body: Мы едем в Латвию через год. — in (a period of time). Мы ездили в Казахстан год назад. — ago. In the first sentence the planned Latvia journey is a year after the reference time; in the second the Kazakhstan journey was a year before it. The forward-looking time construction takes accusative, not genitive; the time noun here has the same surface form as nominative. Ago follows an accusative time expression. The choices classify the shown time relation, not independently produce the whole sentence.

sessions.title: Distinguish time spent from completion within a period

steps.title: Time spent does not assert the task was finished
steps.body: An imperfective verb with a bare accusative time expression states time spent on an activity and does not assert completion. Анна читала статью два часа. — time spent reading without asserting completion. Борис писал письмо час. — time spent writing without asserting completion. These report time devoted to reading or writing. Not asserting completion does not mean asserting that the task was never finished.

steps.title: The completed task and its time frame
steps.body: A perfective verb with an accusative time expression after the preposition states the period within which a bounded task was completed. Анна прочитала статью за два часа. — the article was finished within two hours. Here the perfective reading verb and the completion-time construction present the article as finished within the two-hour period. Contrast that with time spent reading without asserting completion. This completion interval differs from the forward-looking time until the Latvia journey. The current choices classify three supplied sentences; they do not test independently choosing aspect and constructing a time phrase.

sessions.title: Distinguish a negative verb from a negative noun predicate

steps.title: A speaking reply and its negative
steps.body: Да, говорю́ — Yes, I'm speaking. Нет, не говорю́ — No, I'm not speaking. The first word of each reply answers yes or no. The separate negative particle before the speaking verb negates that predicate; it is not merely the initial no reply. The guided choice keeps the speaking action and changes it to a negative reply.

steps.title: A verb and a zero present copula
steps.body: To negate a verb, simply add не (nye) before the verb: the shown examples illustrate this ordinary predicate-negation pattern. In a present-tense noun predicate, the verb corresponding to is is normally omitted. The negative particle can then stand before the noun predicate itself. That is a different structure from a speaking verb with a negative particle.

steps.title: The question and the student statement
steps.body: Вы говори́те? — Are you speaking? Он не студент — He's not a student. The speaking question is not itself negated. The student statement has a noun predicate and no overt present-tense is. The check asks for that negative nominal sentence, not another speaking reply.

steps.title: A complete negative coming sentence
steps.body: Борис не приходит — Boris isn't coming. The negative particle precedes the coming verb. This complete sentence identifies Boris as the subject and coming as the action. The options не студент and не говорю́ are shorter fragments about being a student or speaking; they do not express the complete Boris-coming sentence. These choices recognize supplied structures rather than independently constructing every negative predicate.

sessions.title: Distinguish existence, absence and the negative particle

steps.title: Existence and absence are not yes and no replies
steps.body: есть means exists in the supplied existence pattern. нет expresses absence in its negative counterpart. The same word can also be a no reply, but that conversational use is different from the absence construction. Да is a yes reply. The separate particle не negates a predicate; it is not the standalone replacement for existence in this pattern.

steps.title: The noun after the absence construction
steps.body: If it isn't there, we use нет followed by the genitive. In this construction the person or thing whose existence or possession is denied is expressed in the genitive. Do not replace the existence word with the separate particle and leave the construction unchanged. The checks identify the supplied existence/absence forms, not independently produce a genitive noun phrase.

steps.title: A pronunciation label is not a translation
steps.body: не — nye in the retained example is a pronunciation/transliteration label, not an English meaning. This particle is different from нет expressing absence and from есть asserting existence. A reference cue can be shown while the question asks for a contrasting form; read whether the question asks for existence, absence or ordinary predicate negation.

sessions.title: Keep noun number and case distinct under negation

steps.title: The singular and plural examples used by the checks
steps.body: Я не ви́жу э́ту кни́гу. — I don't see this book, singular. Я не ви́жу кни́гу — I don't see the book. Я не ви́жу книг. — I don't see any books. The first two show a singular accusative object; the last shows a genitive plural object. Negation remains in every sentence. Changing noun form does not turn the statement into a positive one.

steps.title: Genitive is not simply a plural marker
steps.body: A negated direct object can be genitive or accusative depending on meaning, context and usage. Indefinite reference often favors genitive, but this is not a mechanical rule that every negative sentence must use it. The older book ending in the retained source can also be genitive singular or accusative plural; it is not unambiguous genitive plural. The worked example now uses the same explicit plural-genitive phrase as the repaired check. I don't see the one book is still a singular description. I see this book and I see the books are positive descriptions and therefore do not match the negated cues. These choices distinguish supplied meanings and number, not independently choose every case under negation.

sessions.title: Distinguish negative pronouns from absence and indefinite forms

steps.title: Nobody and nothing refer to different categories
steps.body: кто — никто́. что — ничто́. The first pair concerns a person and nobody; the second concerns a thing and nothing. The indefinite options не́кто and не́что refer to an unspecified person or thing, not the corresponding nobody/nothing form. Do not treat a similar-looking prefix as proof of the same meaning.

steps.title: No person available for an action
steps.body: Negative predicative constructions express the absence of a person or thing for an action. The construction selects a case form; it has no nominative form. Compare the indefinite pronoun separately. не́кого спросить — there is nobody to ask. This is absence of a person available for the infinitive action; it differs from an unspecified person and from there is nothing to ask.

steps.title: The case comes from the construction
steps.body: не́кто is an indefinite pronoun, a person whose identity is not specified. It is not the predicative negative of кто. Absence of a person uses a case form: не́кого has the same form in the genitive and accusative, while не́кому is dative and не́кем instrumental. The sentence determines the case; absence meaning alone does not. There is no nominative form in this negative paradigm. The current checks recognize the absence meaning; they do not uniquely identify genitive from the shared genitive/accusative form.

steps.body: Read the requested negative meaning, structure or stated context. Use the complete explanation above. A missed check returns to that full explanation.

steps.title: Review the complete negation contrast
steps.body:
кто — никто́. что — ничто́. The first pair concerns a person and nobody; the second concerns a thing and nothing. The indefinite options не́кто and не́что refer to an unspecified person or thing, not the corresponding nobody/nothing form. Do not treat a similar-looking prefix as proof of the same meaning.

Negative predicative constructions express the absence of a person or thing for an action. The construction selects a case form; it has no nominative form. Compare the indefinite pronoun separately. не́кого спросить — there is nobody to ask. This is absence of a person available for the infinitive action; it differs from an unspecified person and from there is nothing to ask.

не́кто is an indefinite pronoun, a person whose identity is not specified. It is not the predicative negative of кто. Absence of a person uses a case form: не́кого has the same form in the genitive and accusative, while не́кому is dative and не́кем instrumental. The sentence determines the case; absence meaning alone does not. There is no nominative form in this negative paradigm. The current checks recognize the absence meaning; they do not uniquely identify genitive from the shared genitive/accusative form.

sessions.title: Combine negative pronouns with the predicate particle

steps.title: One negative meaning across pronoun and predicate
steps.body: никто́ — не. ничто́ — не. In the supplied negative-concord pattern, the negative pronoun requires the separate negative particle in the predicate. They work together to express one overall negative statement. Do not remove the predicate particle by applying the English idea that two negatives must cancel.

steps.title: A prefix and a whole pronoun are not the predicate particle
steps.body: The option ни- is a pronoun prefix, not the separate predicate particle. никому is a declined pronoun referring to nobody in the dative; it is not that particle either. The answer не is the required predicate particle in the illustrated pattern. The choices recognize this supplied concord rule; they do not test producing every negative pronoun case or all exceptional constructions.

sessions.title: Interpret the supplied persuasion readings in context

steps.title: Two supplied readings with their stated contexts
steps.body: Не надо меня уговаривать. — One should not persuade me in the supplied context where the speaker would never agree. Меня не надо уговаривать. — There is no need to persuade me in the supplied context where the speaker will do it anyway. The questions provide these contexts rather than asking you to infer one unique interpretation from word order alone.

steps.title: Word order is not a universal meaning switch
steps.body: Word order can change what is in focus or in the scope of a particle. It does not by itself assign one unique meaning to every sentence. Intonation and discourse context matter as well. The current source illustrates these two contextual readings; a speaker could use a sentence with a different intended emphasis in another context. The checks recognize the supplied reading, not a universal rule that moving the subject always changes prohibition into lack of necessity.

sessions.title: Distinguish negating the state from negating its experiencer

steps.title: Not cold and not me are different scopes
steps.body: Мне не холодно. — To me it is not cold. This can also be expressed in English as I am not cold. Не мне холодно. — It is not to me that it is cold. The first negates the cold state for the experiencer; the second contrasts the experiencer, so the person who is cold is not me. The second does not by itself identify that other person.

steps.title: Use the demonstrated contrast with its limits
steps.body: Note that the modifier не negates the word which comes right after it. In this supplied pair, its position helps distinguish the state from the experiencer. Wider sentences also depend on construction, emphasis and context; do not apply adjacency as an automatic complete interpretation of every Russian sentence. The check asks for the scope shown in this pair, not free production of every negative-focus construction.

steps.title: Admitted instruction
steps.body: A complete home-delivery address names the recipient, then the premises, then the locality, then the applicable region, then the country, then the postcode.

steps.title: Guided practice
steps.body: A greeting is outside the address, and a letter convention does not identify these components.

steps.title: Admitted instruction
steps.body: Recipient, premises, city, and postcode alone are not the complete order. A district, oblast, krai, or republic is included when that unit applies to the locality. A federal city does not add a separate oblast line. The country names the destination state in this complete order. A post-office box replaces the street line only when that box is the delivery point, and it is not required on every street address. An apartment or office number is included only when the premises has one, and it is omitted when the premises has none.

steps.title: Remediation
steps.body: Return to the complete order: recipient, premises, locality, applicable region, country, and postcode.

steps.title: Independent checks
steps.body: Memorizing one sample line is not the same as organizing the complete address.

provenanceRecords.sourceRecordId: future:In English, when reporting a story, we usually change the tense of what was said
provenanceRecords.shippedText: In English, when reporting a story, we usually change the tense of what was said: compare "I ''am'' English" with "He said he ''was'' English" - the reported verb changes tense. In Russian, however, we keep the tense the same, so the same report is literally, "He said he '''is''' English" - "'''Он сказа́л, что он англича́нин'''", not "'''Он сказа́л, что он ''был'' англича́нином'''".

provenanceRecords.sourceRecordId: date-russia:In [[Russia]], dates are usually written in "day month year" (DMY) order. This o
provenanceRecords.shippedText:
In Russia, dates are usually written in "day month year" (DMY) order. This order is used in both the all-numeric date (for example "28.08.17") and the expanded form (for example "28 августа 2017 г."); the trailing "г" is short for "года" (goda, "of the year"). Coincidentally, in Polish the word for year is "rok", so a similar date format is used by the Poles e.g. 1987r). Single-digit numbers for day or month may have a preceding zero (for example "28.08.2017") is more usual.

When saying the date, it is usually pronounced using the ordinal number of the day first (in neutral grammatical gender), then the month in genitive case (for example "Двадцать восьмое августа").

The complete home-delivery organization names the recipient, then the street with the house and any apartment or office, then the locality, then the district, oblast, krai, or republic when that unit applies, then the country, then the postcode. не́кто is an indefinite pronoun, a person whose identity is not specified. It is not the predicative negative of кто. Absence of a person uses a case form: не́кого has the same form in the genitive and accusative, while не́кому is dative and не́кем instrumental. The sentence determines the case; absence meaning alone does not. There is no nominative form in this negative paradigm.

Possessives such as мо́й and тво́й agree with the noun they describe in gender, number and case. Choose the form from the noun, not from the gender of its owner. Start with the nominative forms below, then compare the feminine accusative example.

In мой стол, стол is masculine singular. In моя собака, собака is feminine singular. Both phrases mean my plus a noun, but the Russian form of my changes to match the noun.

In the nominative singular, мо́й is masculine and моя́ is feminine. For стол choose мо́й; for собака choose моя́. The form follows the noun being described.

моё is the neuter singular nominative form of my. мои́ is the plural nominative form. A singular noun does not take the plural form in these choices.

Наш means our; Ваш means your. In the worked phrase на́ша сестра́, both words are feminine singular nominative. To put this phrase in the direct-object accusative, change both words: на́ша сестра́ becomes на́шу сестру́. Keep the same noun and feminine singular agreement. на́шего бра́та changes the referent, and на́ши is plural.

тво́й is masculine singular nominative; твоя́ is feminine singular nominative. Both mean your. To change the masculine form to the feminine form while keeping nominative singular, choose твоя́.

An adjective agrees with its noun in gender, number and case. In хорошее письмо, the adjective describes a neuter singular noun. хоро́ший is the dictionary form: masculine singular nominative. The following forms belong to the same adjective meaning good.

After ж, ц, ч, ш, or щ, an unstressed о in an ending is written е. That replacement is not a rule for every unstressed о. In хоро́шее, the unstressed ending after ш uses е. The и in хоро́шие follows a different spelling condition: write и rather than ы after ш. Spelling limits the letters in an ending; gender, number and case determine which form is needed.

хоро́шая is feminine singular nominative; хоро́шее is neuter singular nominative. In хоро́шая книга, both words are feminine singular nominative. To put the phrase in the accusative singular, change both words: хоро́шая книга becomes хоро́шую книгу. Keep the same noun and feminine singular agreement. хоро́шего друга is masculine animate; хоро́шие книги is plural.

хоро́шие is plural nominative. To change хоро́шее from neuter singular nominative to plural nominative, choose хоро́шие. To go back to neuter singular, choose хоро́шее. To supply the dictionary form, choose хоро́ший. These choices test the requested form of the adjective; all the options are already correctly spelled.

Adjectives agree with their nouns in gender, number and case. In хорошее письмо, the adjective describes a neuter singular noun. хоро́ший is the dictionary form: masculine singular nominative. This lesson compares singular and plural nominative forms, then explains the spelling in the retained plurals.

After г, к, х, ж, ч, ш, or щ, write и rather than ы. The seven-letter condition is required. This rule applies to the spelling of noun and adjective endings. In кни́ги, и follows г; in хоро́шие, и follows ш. The rule controls spelling, but the question determines the required gender, number and case.

For these nominative checks, кни́га means book in the singular and кни́ги means books in the plural. To form this plural, replace the singular ending with the plural ending: кни́га becomes кни́ги. The stem ends in г, so the seven-letter rule requires и. To return to singular nominative, choose кни́га.

кни́ги is plural nominative in this lesson. дни is also plural nominative and means days. Its и does not follow a letter in the seven-letter set, so дни is not an example of that spelling replacement. Not every plural ending in и comes from the seven-letter rule. Identify number from the requested form and context.

хоро́шее is neuter singular nominative; хоро́шие is plural nominative. To change the neuter singular form to plural nominative, choose хоро́шие; to return to neuter singular, choose хоро́шее. For the masculine singular dictionary form, choose хоро́ший. All these options are correctly spelled: the questions test form recognition rather than choosing between correct and incorrect spellings.

For the saying/telling pair shown here, the perfective counterpart of говори́ть is сказа́ть; the imperfective counterpart of сказа́ть is говори́ть. These checks ask you to recognize this vocabulary pair, not choose aspect in a sentence.

де́лать is imperfective; сде́лать is perfective. Both concern doing or making. The perfective focuses on accomplishing the action; the imperfective can describe the activity or its occurrence without that focus. Given де́лать and a request for its perfective counterpart, choose сде́лать. говори́ть concerns speaking or saying and belongs to the other pair. Learn the shown pair rather than assuming every prefix changes only aspect.

The instrumental case can mark the means used to do something. These checks first teach its forms. сто́л is the dictionary form, meaning table; столо́м is instrumental singular. The word still names a table: the ending marks its grammatical role, not a new vocabulary meaning.

The instrumental singular -ом fits the hard stem of the relevant noun class. Soft stems use their own instrumental ending, so -ом is not universal. Here, keep the stem of сто́л and add -ом to obtain столо́м. Learn the stress with the whole form.

столу́ is dative singular and столе́ is prepositional singular. Both belong to the same noun, but neither has the instrumental singular ending. For an instrumental singular request, select столо́м rather than selecting a form merely because its English gloss is table.

до́м means house in its dictionary form. до́мом is instrumental singular: keep the stem and add -ом. Given до́м and an instrumental singular request, choose до́мом. This is the same ending pattern as the table form.

до́му is dative singular; до́ме is prepositional singular. They do not answer an instrumental singular request. Compare the entire ending with до́мом, and notice that this noun keeps its stem stress.

поездом is instrumental singular of the noun meaning train; карандашом is instrumental singular of the noun meaning pencil. The pencil check asks for that meaning as well as the case. Its other options refer to train and husband. A correct case alone does not identify the requested noun.

книгой is the instrumental singular form for book. This noun has a different ending from the -ом shown for table and house. Do not attach the same ending to every noun. These examples introduce selected singular patterns, not the full instrumental paradigm.

A current-time question and the time when an event happens are different requests. The retained event sentences use at-time expressions. A preposition introduces several of them, while the without construction expresses minutes remaining until the upcoming hour. Study the complete source examples before selecting their readings.

Концерт начинается в шесть часов. — 18.00. Она была дома в час. — 13.00. These are the readings assigned by the retained source. The bare six-hour and one-hour expressions do not themselves distinguish evening from morning; the source readings depend on context. Do not infer that every occurrence of six means eighteen.

Я приду в четверть восьмого. — 7.15 – quarter of the eighth hour. Он нам позвонил в пятнадцать минут десятого. — 9.15 – 15 minutes of the tenth hour. A quarter or fifteen minutes has elapsed in the hour leading to the named next hour. The ordinal is genitive; the event-time phrase also has its introductory preposition.

Наш рейс уезжает в половине пятого. — 4.30 – half of the fifth hour. Мы будем свободны в полвторого. — 1.30 – half of the second hour. Both name a half elapsed in the next ordinal hour. Their retained preposition and noun forms differ; recognize each complete construction rather than exchanging endings mechanically.

Передача начинается без четверти три. — 2.45 – 3 without a quarter. Она обычно приходит на работу без пятнадцати девять. — 8.45 – 9 without 15 minutes. Subtract the stated remaining minutes from the upcoming hour. The preposition meaning without governs the remaining quantity in genitive form. These existing choices do not assess independently building a new event-time sentence.

Которое яблоко моё? — Which apple is mine? Которую книгу вы хотите? — Which book do you want? These are direct questions asking which member is selected, not relative clauses modifying an earlier noun. In the apple question the selecting form agrees with a neuter singular subject in the nominative. In the book question it agrees with a feminine singular direct object in the accusative. Match the whole question: ownership of an apple differs from wanting a book.

полтора́ рубля́ — 1.5 roubles. полторы́ мину́ты — 1.5 minutes. The first numeral form is masculine/neuter; the second is feminine.
